new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word (Shaul: the last syllable of the head word of a phrase, or of a word uttered alone), with lengthening of the consonant or vowel immediately before the stressed syllable (nam:á 'father', kamama:wa). This is Shaul's inference from the accent marks in Piccolo's 1702 spellings of roughly a dozen items (etudá, makabá, nam:á; sentence Taxamà coñit mulas huala endetcù), i.e. the same final-stress pattern he describes for neighbouring Cochimí and Robinia.
new_statements.exceptions: None discussed; several recorded items carry no accent mark (medese, ibo, yexwi/tejui, kamama:wa) and Shaul does not comment on them.
new_statements.domain_note: Shaul frames the domain as the 'head word of a phrase or single-word utterance', i.e. final stress on the phonological word, possibly realized once per close-knit phrase (parallel to his Cochimí analysis). Evidence base is a fragmentary 1702 missionary record (about 11-14 lexical/grammatical items and one sentence); the statement is a philological inference, not an observation of speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Shaul's 'Monqui' is the language of the Loreto (native name Conchó) mission area as recorded by the Jesuit F. M. Piccolo in 1702; the entire corpus is about a dozen words/morphemes, 14 untranslated place names and one sentence. That Piccolo's words are Monqui rather than Cochimí is Shaul's own argument (Piccolo speaks of 'our Monqui language'; Mixco 1978 did not use these items for Cochimí); Massey 1949 took Monqui to be a Cochimí dialect, while Laylander 1997, Golla 2011 and Zamponi 2024 treat it as unclassified/unattested. Glottocode monq1236 is the right match; no dialect distinction is possible.

readall_conflicts: Golla 2011 could not be assessed (copy consulted is front matter only). Zamponi 2024 is silent on Monqui stress; its only nearby stress statement is about Waikuri (unpredictable, probably phonemic root stress) and does not describe Monqui. One indirect tension: Shaul 2020's rule ('stress on the last syllable of the head word of a phrase') rests on his parse of Piccolo's single sentence 'Taxamà coñit mulas huala endetcù', and Zamponi (pp. 101-102) explicitly calls that sentence 'grammatically unanalyzable (pace Shaul 2020: 136-137)', which weakens the phrase-head domain claim, though not the word-final placement itself: every accented form Zamponi reprints from Piccolo, del Barco and Venegas carries its accent on the final vowel.
